title: Scientific Opinion on the risk for public health related to the presence of mercury and methylmercury in food
authors: EFSA Panel on Contaminants in the Food Chain (CONTAM)
funder: European Food Safety Authority, on request from the European Commission (Question No EFSA-Q-2011-00923).
authorConflicts: Declarations of interest of panel members are held by EFSA; not read.
result: Methylmercury is by far the most common form of organic mercury in the food chain; mercury content varied widely among fish species and was highest in predatory fish; tuna, swordfish, cod, whiting and pike were major contributors to adult exposure. Methylmercury is much more extensively and rapidly absorbed than mercuric and mercurous mercury, more than 90% of blood methylmercury is in erythrocytes, and it crosses the placenta and the blood-brain barrier; absorbed methylmercury is excreted mainly in faeces as mercuric mercury. On the basis of prenatal exposure and neurodevelopmental outcomes, the Panel established a tolerable weekly intake for methylmercury of 1.3 µg/kg body weight, expressed as mercury, against the JECFA provisional tolerable weekly intake of 1.6 µg/kg. The 95th percentile dietary exposure is close to or above the TWI for all age groups; high fish consumers, which might include pregnant women, may exceed it by up to approximately six-fold; unborn children are the most vulnerable group. The opinion does not assess the nutritional benefits of fish.
